questions.question: A kitchen backsplash panel is one whole rectangle divided into 8 equal square tiles (2 rows of 4). Every tile holds the same leaf shape: 3 of the tiles show the leaf slid straight across (a translation), and the other 5 show the leaf turned a half turn (a rotation). There are no gaps and no overlaps. What fraction of the whole panel was covered using translations?
questions.explain: The whole panel is 8 equal parts, and 3 of those parts were made by sliding, so the answer is 3/8. The common trap is writing 3/5, which compares the slid tiles to the turned tiles instead of to the whole panel.

questions.question: A quilt block is one whole square divided into 9 equal small squares (3 rows of 3). The same L-shaped piece is sewn into every small square, and each copy is slid straight across from the one beside it, so all 9 copies face the same way with no gaps and no overlaps. Which statement best explains the pattern?
options: It is not a tessellation, because only regular shapes such as squares and hexagons can tessellate.
It is a tessellation, and the L-shaped piece was repeated by translations (slides).
It is a tessellation, and the L-shaped piece was repeated by rotations of 90 degrees.
It is not a tessellation, because every copy faces the same way instead of being turned or flipped.
questions.explain: A tessellation is identical copies covering a surface with no gaps or overlaps, and here each copy is moved by a slide, which is a translation. Two common traps are thinking only regular polygons can tessellate and thinking the copies must be turned or flipped.

questions.question: A hallway floor is one whole rectangle covered by 24 equal square tiles arranged in 4 rows and 6 columns. A boot-print stencil is stamped on every tile. In columns 1, 3 and 5 the stencil is stamped as it is; in columns 2, 4 and 6 the stencil is stamped flipped over (a reflection). How many of the 24 tiles show the reflected stencil?
questions.explain: Three of the six columns are reflected, and each column holds 4 tiles, so 3 x 4 = 12 tiles. The common trap is answering 3, which counts the reflected columns instead of the reflected tiles.

questions.question: A placemat is one whole rectangle divided into 10 equal triangles that meet with no gaps and no overlaps. Six of the triangles show a fish design in its starting position, and 4 of them show the same fish design rotated a half turn. What fraction of the whole placemat was covered using rotations?
questions.explain: The rotated copies fill 4 of the 10 equal parts of the whole, and 4/10 simplifies to 2/5. The common trap is writing 4/6, which compares the rotated triangles to the unrotated ones rather than to the whole placemat.

questions.question: Ella has many identical copies of a quadrilateral tile whose angles measure 85 degrees, 95 degrees, 100 degrees and 80 degrees. She rotates every second copy a half turn so that at each meeting point one of each of the four angles comes together. Why do four tiles fit around that point with no gap and no overlap?
options: The four angles of the quadrilateral add to 360 degrees, so one of each angle exactly fills the full turn.
The four angles add to 180 degrees, and 180 degrees is a full turn.
All four sides of the tile are the same length, so the tiles match up.
Opposite angles of the tile are equal, so the copies line up.
questions.explain: The angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees (85 + 95 + 100 + 80 = 360), and a full turn around a point is also 360 degrees, so one of each angle fills the point. The usual trap is using 180 degrees, which is the angle sum of a triangle or a straight line, not a full turn.

questions.question: On a coordinate grid, a floor tile has vertices at (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 3) and (0, 3). The next tile in the tessellation has vertices at (4, 0), (8, 0), (8, 3) and (4, 3). Which single transformation maps the first tile onto the second?
options: A reflection in the y-axis
A translation of 4 units right
A rotation of 90 degrees about the origin
A translation of 3 units right
questions.explain: Every vertex gains 4 on the x-coordinate and keeps its y-coordinate, so the tile slides 4 units right, which is a translation. The common trap is sliding 3 units, which uses the height of the tile instead of its width.

questions.question: A regular pentagon has interior angles of 108 degrees. Sam wants to tile a games-room floor with identical regular pentagon tiles, fitting them around a single point. What happens?
options: Four pentagons fit around the point and leave a 72 degree gap.
Three pentagons fit exactly, because 3 x 108 = 360, so they do tessellate.
Three pentagons fit and leave a 36 degree gap, so regular pentagons do not tessellate.
Three pentagons fit and leave a 36 degree gap, but flipping every second pentagon closes it.
questions.explain: Three pentagons give 3 x 108 = 324 degrees, and 360 - 324 = 36 degrees is left over, so the tiles cannot cover the point. The common trap is assuming a flip or a turn can close a gap, but reflections and rotations never change the size of an angle.

questions.question: Mia has a large pile of identical scalene triangle tiles (no equal sides, no right angle) for a mosaic board at her school. Which plan will cover the board with no gaps and no overlaps?
options: Only triangles with a right angle can tessellate, so no plan will work.
Slide every copy in the same direction and keep the same orientation, since identical triangles always meet edge to edge.
Enlarge every second triangle so its edges match the first one.
Rotate a copy a half turn about the midpoint of one side to make a parallelogram, then translate that parallelogram again and again.
questions.explain: A half-turn rotation about the midpoint of a side joins two copies into a parallelogram, and parallelograms tile by simple slides, so every triangle tessellates. The common trap is sliding copies in the same orientation only, which leaves triangular gaps between the rows.

questions.question: A community centre lobby is tiled with identical quadrilateral tiles. Going around one tile, three of its angles measure 70 degrees, 100 degrees and 65 degrees. The tiles are laid so that one of each of the four angles meets at every corner point. What is the fourth angle, and why does the pattern have no gaps?
options: 125 degrees, and the four different angles meet at each point and add to 360 degrees, so no gap is left.
125 degrees, but the tiles will overlap, because 4 x 125 = 500, which is more than 360 degrees.
100 degrees, because the angle opposite the 100 degree angle must be equal to it.
125 degrees, but the tile cannot tessellate, because its sides are not all the same length.
questions.explain: The angles of a quadrilateral add to 360 degrees, so the fourth angle is 360 - (70 + 100 + 65) = 125 degrees, and because one of each different angle meets at a point, they total 360 degrees exactly. The common trap is thinking the same angle meets four times, or that a tile needs equal sides to tessellate.

questions.question: A garden path in Surrey is paved with identical kite-shaped concrete tiles. Every second row of tiles is turned a half turn, so the tiles do not all face the same way, but there are no gaps and no overlaps anywhere on the path. Noah says this is not a real tessellation, because the tiles are not all facing the same way and a kite is not a regular polygon. Which response is correct?
options: Noah is right, because only regular polygons such as squares and hexagons can tessellate, and a kite has sides of two different lengths.
Noah is wrong: rotating copies is allowed, since a tessellation only needs identical copies covering the surface with no gaps or overlaps.
Noah is right, because every tile in a tessellation must face the same way, so turning every second row breaks the repeating pattern.
Noah is wrong, but the pattern counts only if every second row is also reflected in a mirror line, since a half turn on its own is not enough.
questions.explain: A tessellation is defined by identical shapes covering a surface with no gaps or overlaps, and translations, rotations and reflections may all be used to place the copies. The common trap is believing tiles must be regular polygons or must all point the same way.

questions.question: A family is choosing patio stones. The regular hexagon stones have interior angles of 120 degrees, and the regular octagon stones have interior angles of 135 degrees. They want a patio covered with only one type of stone, with no gaps and no cutting. Which should they choose, and why?
options: Either one, because every regular polygon tessellates as long as all the stones are the same size, since equal edges always line up.
The octagons, because 135 degrees is larger, so each stone covers more of the point and fewer stones are needed to fill the 360 degrees.
The hexagons, because three meet exactly at a point (3 x 120 = 360), while two octagons cover only 270 degrees and leave a 90 degree gap.
The octagons, because three of them fit exactly (3 x 135 = 360), and bigger angles fill the space around a point more quickly.
questions.explain: Check whether the interior angle divides evenly into the 360 degrees around a point: 360 divided by 120 is exactly 3, but 360 divided by 135 is not a whole number, so two octagons leave 360 - 270 = 90 degrees of gap. The common trap is assuming any regular polygon tessellates, or slipping to 3 x 135 = 360 instead of 405.

questions.question: For an art project, Kai starts with a square tile 10 cm by 10 cm. He cuts a curved bump with an area of 6 square centimetres out of the left edge and slides that exact piece (a translation) straight across to stick onto the right edge. He then repeats the new tile across the page. What is true about the new tile?
options: Its area is 94 square centimetres, so small gaps will be left in the pattern, because cutting 6 square centimetres out of the edge makes the tile smaller than before.
Its area is 106 square centimetres, so the tiles will overlap, because sticking a 6 square centimetre bump onto the right edge makes the tile bigger than the square.
Its area is 100 square centimetres, but it cannot tessellate, because it is no longer a polygon like a square, and only straight sides can fit together with no gaps.
Its area is 100 square centimetres, and it still tessellates, because the piece removed from the left edge exactly fills the space it was added to on the right.
questions.explain: Cutting 6 square centimetres off one edge and sliding the same piece onto the opposite edge gives 100 - 6 + 6 = 100 square centimetres, and the translated bump fits into the notch of the next tile, so the pattern still has no gaps. The common trap is thinking a shape must be a polygon, or subtracting the 6 without adding it back on.
